_note: Offline demo corpus of real, well-known papers on LLM agents. Titles, first authors, years and arXiv ids match the published papers; author lists are abbreviated and abstracts are short paraphrases written for this project, not the authors' text. Consult the URL for the original abstract before citing any paper.

papers.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce reasoning traces and can also generate actions, but these abilities are usually studied separately. ReAct interleaves reasoning steps with task-specific actions such as calls to a Wikipedia API. Reasoning helps the model plan and update its plan, while actions let it gather external information. On question answering and interactive decision-making benchmarks the approach reduces hallucination and improves interpretability compared with reasoning-only or acting-only baselines.

papers.title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
papers.abstract: Language models struggle with arithmetic, factual lookup and other tasks that simple external tools solve easily. Toolformer is trained in a self-supervised way to decide which API to call, when to call it and how to use the result. Only a handful of demonstrations per tool are needed. The model improves zero-shot performance on several downstream tasks while keeping its core language modelling ability.

papers.title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
papers.abstract: Generative agents are computational agents that simulate believable human behaviour in an interactive sandbox environment. The architecture stores a complete record of experiences in natural language memory, synthesises memories into higher-level reflections, and retrieves them dynamically to plan behaviour. An evaluation shows that observation, planning and reflection each contribute to believable individual and emergent social behaviour.

papers.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reflexion reinforces language agents through linguistic feedback rather than weight updates. After each trial the agent reflects verbally on task feedback and stores the reflection in an episodic memory buffer. The stored reflections guide better decisions in later trials. The method improves results on sequential decision-making, coding and language reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Generating a chain of intermediate reasoning steps significantly improves the ability of large language models to perform complex reasoning. Chain-of-thought prompting supplies a few worked examples with reasoning steps in the prompt. The benefit emerges with sufficiently large models. Experiments on arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning benchmarks show substantial gains.

papers.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Left-to-right token generation limits language models on tasks that need exploration or lookahead. Tree of Thoughts generalises chain-of-thought prompting by exploring coherent units of text as intermediate steps in a search tree. The model self-evaluates choices and can backtrack, using breadth-first or depth-first search. Planning-heavy tasks such as the Game of 24 and creative writing improve markedly.

papers.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
papers.abstract: AutoGen is an open-source framework for building applications in which multiple conversable agents cooperate to accomplish tasks. Agents can combine language models, human input and tools. Developers define agent interaction behaviours with both natural language and code. Case studies cover mathematics, coding, question answering and decision-making.

papers.title: A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents
papers.abstract: This survey reviews research on autonomous agents built on large language models. It proposes a unified framework covering profiling, memory, planning and action modules. It summarises applications in social science, natural science and engineering, and common evaluation strategies. It closes with open challenges and future directions for the field.

papers.title: HuggingGPT: Solving AI Tasks with ChatGPT and its Friends in Hugging Face
papers.abstract: HuggingGPT uses a large language model as a controller that connects many specialised machine learning models from Hugging Face. The controller performs task planning from the user request, selects models by their descriptions, executes subtasks and summarises the results. This lets one system tackle complex multi-modal tasks across language, vision and speech.

papers.title: Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning by Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting suffers from calculation errors, missing steps and semantic misunderstanding. Plan-and-Solve prompting first asks the model to devise a plan that divides the task into subtasks, then to carry out the subtasks according to the plan. Variants add more detailed instructions. The approach outperforms zero-shot chain-of-thought across arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning datasets.

papers.title: Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
papers.abstract: Like people, language models do not always produce their best output on the first attempt. Self-Refine has a single model generate an output, critique it with feedback, and refine it iteratively. It needs no supervised training data or reinforcement learning. Outputs improve across diverse tasks from dialogue to code optimisation.

papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
papers.abstract: Large pre-trained language models store factual knowledge in their parameters but cannot easily update it or show provenance. Retrieval-augmented generation combines a parametric sequence-to-sequence model with a non-parametric memory, a dense vector index of Wikipedia accessed by a neural retriever. The models generate more specific and factual language than parametric-only baselines. They set strong results on open-domain question answering.

papers.title: MetaGPT: Meta Programming for A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems built on language models can suffer from cascading hallucinations when agents chain their outputs naively. MetaGPT encodes standardised operating procedures into prompt sequences so agents with specialised roles produce structured intermediate outputs. Role specialisation and an assembly-line workflow reduce errors. Software engineering benchmarks show more coherent solutions than chat-based multi-agent baselines.

papers.title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for "Mind" Exploration of Large Language Model Society
papers.abstract: CAMEL studies how communicative agents can cooperate autonomously to complete tasks. It introduces role-playing, where inception prompting guides an assistant agent and a user agent towards task completion while staying consistent with human intentions. The framework generates conversational data for studying the behaviour and capabilities of multi-agent societies.

papers.title: LLM+P: Empowering Large Language Models with Optimal Planning Proficiency
papers.abstract: Large language models are poor at solving long-horizon planning problems reliably. LLM+P translates a natural-language planning problem into the Planning Domain Definition Language, calls a classical planner to find an optimal plan, and translates the plan back into natural language. On benchmark planning domains this produces correct plans far more often than the language model alone.

papers.title: Understanding the planning of LLM agents: A survey
papers.abstract: This survey gives a systematic view of planning in agents built on large language models. It groups existing work into task decomposition, plan selection, external planner modules, reflection and memory. Each category is analysed for strengths and weaknesses. The survey discusses open challenges for planning capability in language agents.

papers.title: The Rise and Potential of Large Language Model Based Agents: A Survey
papers.abstract: This survey traces the concept of agents from philosophy to artificial intelligence and argues that large language models are suitable foundations for general agents. It presents a framework with brain, perception and action components. It reviews single-agent, multi-agent and human-agent cooperation applications, and discusses agent societies, trustworthiness and open problems.

papers.title: Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation
papers.abstract: Natural language generation models often produce text that is unfaithful to the source or factually wrong, known as hallucination. This survey reviews metrics, mitigation methods and future directions for hallucination. It covers task-specific findings in summarisation, dialogue, question answering and other generation tasks. Hallucination is a key obstacle to deploying generation systems safely.

papers.title: WebGPT: Browser-assisted question-answering with human feedback
papers.abstract: WebGPT fine-tunes a language model to answer long-form questions by searching and navigating a text-based web browser. The model must collect references while browsing to support its answers, which makes factual accuracy easier to evaluate. Training uses imitation learning followed by optimisation against a reward model learned from human preferences.

papers.title: Communicative Agents for Software Development
papers.abstract: ChatDev is a virtual software company in which language-model agents with roles such as programmer, reviewer and tester collaborate through chat. Development follows a waterfall-style chain of design, coding, testing and documentation phases. Communication between agents helps identify and fix bugs. The system produces complete software at low cost.
